stories.title_en: Boatmen Abscond with a Servant and the Luggage

paragraphs.en: Assistant Magistrate Ni had risen from the clerical ranks; his family was in fact extremely wealthy. Newly appointed and about to leave for his post, he bought household goods, curios, and bolts of silk in the capital—every piece fine and beautiful—and packed them as six loads of luggage. When all was ready, he first sent three servants to the riverbank to hire a boat. One stayed on board to watch the luggage; the other two came back. The next day Assistant Magistrate Ni and the rest of the party went to the river to find the boat, but the earlier boat was nowhere to be seen. No one knew where the watching servant had been taken; they knew a rogue boatman had swindled them away with the goods.

Assistant Magistrate Ni had no choice but to return to the capital and borrow travel funds from fellow provincials, intending to file a charge at a capital yamen to have the boat thieves caught. Fellow provincials stopped him, saying: “Whenever you hire a boat, you must book it at a registered wharf so the helmsman has a name that can be checked; only then is it safe. If you hire a boat yourself at the river’s edge, neither side knows the other, and there is no background to check—how can you avoid disaster? Besides, pirate boats often lurk along the river. Their helmsmen disguise themselves as merchants, find out which vessel carries good cargo, and then rob it midstream. All such cases are discovered by checking at the office first. If you do not know this and board their boat by mistake, even the master himself may be harmed—how much more when they carry off a single servant! You have a deadline to take up your post; how can you wait here long? The boat thieves have no names and leave no trail; even if you file a charge, where would you hunt them? Better drop it.” Assistant Magistrate Ni took the advice, bought the most needful things again in the capital, and hurried off to his post. This is a case of not knowing how to book a boat and thus coming to grief; it is recorded as a warning for those who travel by water.

stories.title_en: A Concubine Stolen from the Boat by Night

paragraphs.en: In Yangzhou there was a crook named Wei, who lived by running swindles. He had a daughter, Miss Wei, pretty and clever, just sixteen, not yet betrothed. A partner in the same racket, a young sharp named Ji, had no parents at home; Wei therefore took him as a live-in son-in-law. Husband and wife loved each other, and father-in-law and son-in-law were of one mind.

For half a year after that, there was little business. It happened that Magistrate Jia, newly appointed and on his way to his post, passed through Yangzhou and wanted to take a concubine. Wei and his son-in-law Ji discussed it privately and decided to palm the daughter off on him in a sham marriage. Ji agreed, acted as matchmaker himself, and went to discuss it with Magistrate Jia. Jia came to look, was pleased, sent betrothal gifts at once, paid eighty taels, and chose a day for the wedding. Wei and Ji together said to the daughter: "We have had no business for half a year; the household is hard pressed, so we are marrying you to Magistrate Jia in name only. In truth your husband is a young man—how could he bear to give you up? We are your parents, and we have only you—how could we bear to let you go? We simply have no choice; we are treating you as merchandise. Besides, Magistrate Jia is old; he has not brought his principal wife with him for now, so of course he will cherish you. But I fear that after he takes up his post and sends for the principal wife, she will surely treat you cruelly; cursing and whipping will be hard to avoid. The old saying goes: 'Better a poor man's wife than a rich man's concubine.' For now we will send you; in a few days he will board a boat. Your husband will secretly follow in a boat, with a white pair of trousers hung up as a signal. If you can get away at night, cross over to the white-trousers boat; your husband will be there to take you. Do not oversleep and ruin your husband's whole life; you yourself would also suffer." Ji deliberately clutched his wife's clothes, weeping, and pleaded to her face: "If you will promise to come back, I will let you go; if you cannot get away, I would rather die with you—I cannot bear to part." His wife Miss Wei also wept and said: "When father and mother have given the order, how would I not come back? Only you must follow in a boat and wait to take me; do not miss the time." The three of them had the plan set.

The next day Magistrate Jia sent men to fetch the bride. Ji, acting as the matchmaker, saw them off; Jia and Miss Wei consummated their marriage at an inn. The following day, Wei hosted a feast for his son-in-law to see him off on his journey. On the fourth day, Jia and his wife packed and boarded the boat, while Wei and Ji saw them off with great diligence. The boat traveled one day without incident, then moored at a sandbar the next. Ji secretly followed in another boat, drew up alongside, and hung a white pair of trousers from its mast. Miss Wei went out to the bow with her husband Jia to look around; seeing the boat with the white trousers nearby, she knew Ji was waiting. That night, she slept with Jia, being particularly tender, and they enjoyed themselves fully. Being older and newly married, Jia had not missed a night's pleasure; moreover, having spent himself once more on the boat that night, he fell into a deep, snoring sleep. Miss Wei then rose quietly, crawled across to the boat marked by the white trousers. Ji had been waiting long; they were overjoyed to meet, like a flower blooming again and the moon becoming full once more. Under cover of night, they poled away and fled home.

The next morning Magistrate Jia woke and did not see Miss Wei; he was much puzzled and suspicious. He then sent a servant to report it at Old Wei’s house. The Wei family acted startled, suspecting a quarrel on the boat had driven her to throw herself in the water. They went at once to the prefecture and filed a charge of cruelty driving a person to drown. After several days the servant came back to report. Magistrate Jia had a deadline to take up his post and could not wait long; he did not go to plead his side, but went straight to his post. Three years later he went to the capital for the imperial audience, and sent a servant with a few ceremonial gifts to Old Wei. The servant saw that the house had a young woman holding a small child, the very image of Miss Wei, and rushed back to tell his master. When Magistrate Jia went in a sedan, there was no trace of her. He asked who yesterday’s woman was; Wei said: “My wife’s sister’s daughter.” Wei’s wife then came out weeping, questioning and cursing, grabbing him and demanding he produce the person; he was cheated of another ten taels before he could get away. This is a case of wrongly taking a trickster’s daughter: he lost both the woman and the money, and swallowed no small amount of trouble besides.

Note: He took a concubine from her father’s house; they consummated the marriage at an inn and saw her off as she boarded the boat—one would call it perfectly secure. Who knew that later, on the boat, she could still slip away at night? Thus, when taking a concubine from outside, one must not only scrutinize the girl’s family but also investigate where the matchmaker lives, and have the innkeeper join in verifying the facts to avoid loss. Still, generally speaking, it is safer to take a local girl.

stories.title_en: Boatmen Murder a Merchant Buying Copper Goods

paragraphs.en: Luo Siwei was from Linhuai County, Fengyang Prefecture, Nanjing. Accompanied by his servant Cheng Sanlang, he took over a hundred taels to Songjiang to buy cotton cloth, sold it in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian, then went to Chong'an to buy bamboo shoots. That year, shoots were scarce and expensive, so he used the silver there to purchase blackened copperware, along with laminated cups, plates, and other copper vessels. He packed them in bamboo chests, making three loads with his luggage. From Chong'an, he hired porters all the way to Chen Si's shop at Shuikou to book a boat. There, he unexpectedly met his cousin Lin Zida, also staying at this shop. Zida asked: "What goods have you bought?" Siwei replied: "Just some copperware to take away, plus cups and plates I intend to keep for household use." Zida and the broker Chen Si arranged a fast narrow boat for him. The helmsman Lai Fuer and sailors Li Cai and Weng Jide loaded his luggage onto the boat; it was very heavy. The helmsman suspected it contained gold and silver, and a wicked thought arose. Once aboard, he refused to take any other passengers. Siwei said: "I want to leave quickly—why not take others?" The helmsman replied: "It is nearly evening. Tomorrow we will take a few more passengers before setting sail." Siwei instructed Sanlang to buy wine and food for the night. The helmsman and the two sailors discussed: "If we miss the chance tonight, tomorrow it will be too late to act." Siwei and his servant drank until drunk and fell into deep sleep. After midnight, the helmsman moved the boat to a secluded spot; the three men stabbed the master and servant to death with knives and threw their bodies into the river. They broke open the loads and inspected: it was copperware, with only fifteen taels of ready silver remaining. Fuer said: "I insisted it was all silver—a fortune for us three! And now it turns out to be this stuff!" Cai said: "Such fine goods are still worth a considerable amount of silver." Fuer asked: "Where can we sell them?" Cai replied: "Why worry about a place to sell? Mooring the boat somewhere and selling along the way—who wouldn't buy?"

It was already three months after Lin Zida had parted from Siwei when he reached home and paid a visit to Siwei. Siwei’s father said: “My son went out and has not yet come back.” Zida said: “That cannot be right! Three months ago I met him at broker Chen Si’s shop at Shuikou in Jiangxi. I went with the broker to hire a boat for him. He said he had bought copper goods in Fujian, packed in bamboo chests as three loads, and was coming straight home to this place to sell them. Could it be the helmsman meant harm?” Before he had finished, father, mother, wife, and the whole house burst into tears. Zida said: “Do not cry yet. He may still be selling along the way, for all we know. Or if the helmsman meant harm, he would have to sell the copper in various places. Try tracing the copper in the shops, ask where it came from, and the matter will be clear. Even if the copper leaves no trace, go on to broker Chen Si’s at Shuikou, find the helmsman and question him, and you will surely get to the bottom of it.” Siwei’s father agreed, and told his second son Luo Kui to go with Zida to inquire.

They inquired all the way to Wuhu County. Seeing the copperware in a shop there, they asked, "Did you buy this copperware yourself, or did another merchant bring it here to sell?" The shopkeeper replied, "Three months ago, three travelers came and sold it." Zida asked, "Where were they from?" "From Jiangxi," he said. Alarmed, Zida said, "Then I was mistaken—my cousin really did meet with foul play!" He and Kui went straight to Shuikou and asked Chen Si, "Which county was the boat captain who loaded my cousin's goods from?" Chen Si replied, "From Yanshan County." Zida told him what had happened, and went with Chen Si to Yanshan to have the men arrested.

At that time, Li Cai and Weng Jide had sold the copperware, held the silver in hand, and each went to a brothel to spend it. Lin and Chen spotted Cai and hid. Lin Zida said: "He is enjoying himself in the house; he will not be in a hurry to move. You and I will go to the county office to file a charge, have constables sent to arrest them, so they cannot escape." The two entered the county office; the charge was accepted. Magistrate Chen dispatched six constables, who accompanied Lin and Chen to the brothel to make the arrest. Cai and Jide were just laughing and drinking with the prostitutes when Chen pointed them out to the constables, and both were seized and shackled. They then went to Lai Fu's house; Fu was just stepping out elsewhere, encountered them, and was also caught. The three were taken together before the official. Magistrate Chen interrogated them, subjected them to the ankle press and beatings; unable to endure the pain, they confessed. Cai said: "When we moved the chests onto the boat, they were extraordinarily heavy. We suspected gold and silver, so the three of us formed the intent to kill them and threw the bodies into the river. We opened the chests and found only copperware, with fifteen taels of ready silver. Regret came too late. The copper was sold along the way; the silver has already been divided. Now the affair is exposed; we brought this upon ourselves and willingly admit to a capital crime." Magistrate Chen ordered each of the three to receive fifty strokes, then sentenced them to death; the stolen goods were recovered and given to Luo Kui and Lin Zida to take home. The two kowtowed and departed.

Note: Streams and rivers are inherently dangerous places, and helmsmen are often coarse, violent men. If you carry ready silver on you, you must hide it deep and watch it strictly. If you carry copper, lead, tin, and the like—heavy things that resemble silver—you must tell them plainly, open the loads and show them, so they will not drool, and only then will you be safe. Otherwise it is like shooting sparrows with gold pellets, or letting coix seeds pass for pearls: few will escape a villain’s greedy eye. As for avenging the feud, it was still fortunate that the one who succeeded found the root of the matter. Had they not used the man who booked the boat to track down the helmsman, how could they have wiped out the guilty and cut off the evil? But punishing the wicked is no match for keeping yourself safe; a death repaid is no match for coming home alive. So those who travel and carry heavy goods should take a lesson from this, be careful and keep things close, and they will never come to grief.

stories.title_en: Mirrors on the Boat Invite a Murder Plot

paragraphs.en: Xiong Hao of Zhangfu was a scion of a hereditary official family. He possessed strength sufficient to wrestle a tiger and was skilled in staff fighting. One moonlit night, he took two maids into the back garden when a tiger leaped over the wall. He immediately retreated indoors, where each person grabbed a steel fork or a heavy staff before rushing out. The tiger sprang at them head-on; Hao blocked it with his fork, pinned it to the ground, and struck once. The tiger lunged again; Hao pinned it once more with the fork and struck another blow, after which the tiger turned and fled. Hao chased from behind and beat it until it fell. He urgently called to the two maids: "Come help at once!" Each maid wielded a heavy staff, and together they battered the beast until it died beneath their blows. People of the time hailed him as "Fourth Master Hao the Tiger-Beater."

Later he decided to tour all the famous places, so he told his elder brother, making up an excuse: "I am going out to trade." His brother stopped him: "You are stubborn and have no cunning. Do not think of making money; I fear you will only make trouble." Hao said: "The old servant Man Qi has strength and much wit; if he goes with me, what harm?" His brother could not stop him. Hao took a little more than a hundred taels and set out, saying: "I will go out and buy goods as the chance comes. Even if I make no profit, how should I lose the capital? Who can take advantage of me?" When they toured Zhejiang and Guangdong, and there were goods worth buying, the servant Man Qi said: "This price is very cheap; if we buy and take it home we will surely profit." Hao said: "I have come a long way and have not yet seen all the sights here. If I buy goods at once, how can I travel light and free?" The servant urged him repeatedly, but was never heard; he knew his master's mind was on idle touring, not on profit, and afterward only let him be: when the master drank, he drank; when the master went, he followed. In less than half a year two thirds of the capital was gone. Qi said again: "If we do not head home we will have no travel money." Hao said: "Though the capital is small, we still must buy some goods to take back, to serve as gifts after a long journey." They delayed another two months and reached Huzhou; Qi again urged him to head home. Hao said: "What should we buy?" Qi said: "Brushes and ink are best." Hao said: "I am not in that trade and cannot choose; I fear I will be taken advantage of. We also need to buy something for Mother, my sister-in-law, and my wife. The capital is already lost; let us spare them the gossip." Qi said: "Fine silks and mirrors would be good." Hao said: "We have not much capital for silks; we are not that kind of merchant. Better buy ten taels' worth of brushes and ink and ten taels' worth of mirrors." Qi said: "That will do too." They hurried the purchase for the return; there were only two small chests. Hao said: "These goods are excellent, and also light and easy to carry."

When they boarded the boat at the riverbank, the helmsman saw the rich man's imposing bearing and his well-dressed servants, yet their luggage consisted of only two small chests. Once lifted aboard, he felt how heavy the chests were and assumed they must be filled entirely with silver. So he probed with words: "Where have you come from, sir? And why did you not buy more goods?" Hao, fearing that other merchants would look down on him due to his meager capital, lied: "My elder brother holds a humble post in Huguang. I am returning from his office and bought little." The helmsman said, "So you are a young gentleman of an official house." He also observed the servants serving him with great respect, always addressing their master as "Young Master," and noted his lavish spending habits, which set him apart from ordinary merchants; thus, he became even more convinced that he was truly a noble official's son, and everyone on the boat deferred to him. When they reached shore, the other merchants disembarked. The helmsman alone kept Young Gentleman Xiong, saying, "There were many guests on the boat; I could not show you proper respect. I have prepared a cup of wine; please let me invite you." He went ashore, bought fine dishes and good wine, and pressed them to drink late into the night, showing great attentiveness. Xiong Hao drank freely. The helmsman then hard-pressed the servant to drink. Man Qi knew in his heart it was not kindly meant. At first he pretended to refuse; later, unable to resist the urging, he drank several cups, then feigned drunkenness and went to lie down. Young Xiong, trusting the helmsman's coaxing, fell truly drunk and knew nothing. When Qi saw he was sound asleep, he got up and said to the helmsman: "I am not truly drunk. We are near home now; my heart is heavy, and I cannot get the wine down. This young master is a debauched wastrel. The elder master, in his post, sent him home with several hundred taels. On the road he spent it all on whoring; he is only taking a few brushes and a few mirrors home as customary gifts for his nephews. When we get home tomorrow, the old master will surely blame me for not stopping him. There are men like this in the world: they see wine as sugar and love to boast—how can I check him? Let me open the two chests and show you: is there a speck of silver in them?" He took the key and opened both chests: only brushes and mirrors, no silver at all. Qi took two mirrors and gave them to the helmsman, saying, "All along the way you have looked after us; I give each of you a mirror to use." The helmsman said, "A master's things must not be given away." Qi replied, "Take half; he will not be able to count them, and once we are home he will not know the difference." He locked the chests again, went with the helmsman to sleep, and kept watch all night. The next day they went ashore. Hao said, "It is rare for a helmsman to be so kind; give him another qian of silver."

When they reached home, Qi said: "Count the mirrors carefully—make sure none are missing." Hao checked and replied: "Two are gone." Qi said: "I traded those two mirrors for our heads to get us back home. Does the master still not understand?" Hao asked: "Why such wild talk?" Qi then recounted the entire incident on the boat, explaining: "If he intended no harm, why would he spend so much extra on wine and food for people he was about to part with, showing such attentiveness?" Hao exclaimed in alarm: "Exactly! Had you not understood the situation, we would have nearly lost our lives!" The whole household heard this and rejoiced, rewarding Man Qi generously.

Note: Hao was a pampered son of a wealthy house; he took indulging his nature as pleasure and boasting as distinction, never knowing how dangerous the world’s roads are. Had Man Qi not had a clear mind, two lives would have been cast into the fish-bellies. Whenever one travels far, if the master is careless and slack, securing even one close, careful servant brings great benefit. Thus, in the Travel hexagram, losing a servant is an omen of trouble, while gaining one is auspicious. How great is the Sage’s teaching on Travel!

stories.title_en: Luggage Carried onto the Wrong Boat

paragraphs.en: Lu Menglin was from Jinxian, Jiangxi. He traveled to Haicheng County in Fujian to buy over ten loads of pepper, then went to Wuhu to sell them. A fellow merchant swapped one load for borax; the rest was paid in silver. The next day, he had the innkeeper book Helmsman Chen Yasi's boat all the way to Jianning. All the goods were loaded onto the boat, except for one servant, Zhan Xing, who carried a heavy load of packed luggage and followed Menglin. On the road, they suddenly met a fellow townsman who began asking about family affairs, chattering incessantly. Menglin ordered the servant to carry the luggage onto the boat first, then return to wait for further orders. The servant took the load to another boat, stowed it in the cabin, and returned to find his master still deep in conversation with the townsman. Seeing the servant arrive, Menglin sent him off on another errand before taking leave of the townsman and heading to the boat. Upon checking, he found the luggage missing, so he beat and cursed the servant. He also accused the helmsman of stealing more than a hundred taels of silver from the pepper sales, using innkeeper Zhu Nianjiu as a witness. The helmsman protested: "There are over a dozen merchants on this boat; who saw your servant carry luggage aboard?" Magistrate Hu summoned everyone to hear the case. All the other merchants testified that they had never seen any luggage being carried on. Magistrate Hu said, "A boat does not lose even a needle. All other goods are present; only the luggage containing silver has vanished?" He subjected the helmsman to the press. The man refused to confess, saying: "It was your servant Zhan Xing who saw the silver in the bundle, stole it himself to frame me; or perhaps he carried it onto the wrong boat by mistake, leading to its loss. Even if you torture this humble man to death, I will not confess!" Magistrate Hu then interrogated Zhan Xing: "I suspect you mistook another boat for your own, and in your haste lost the luggage; it was not that you betrayed your master. Confess properly and you will be spared the press." Zhan Xing refused to confess, so he was pressed and beaten a hundred times. Unable to endure the pain, he finally confessed: "My master met a fellow townsman on the road and was talking. I carried the luggage onto a boat myself, stowed it in the cabin, then returned to wait for my master's orders. When I got back to the boat, the luggage was gone. I mistakenly thought it was our boat, and thus lost it. Fearing my master would punish me severely, I dared not admit it. I beg Your Honor to spare this humble man's life." Magistrate Hu ordered Zhan Xing to receive thirty strokes and advised Menglin: "This was your own fault. Whenever you travel to trade, silver and goods must never leave your side. When carrying luggage, you should have instructed Zhan Xing to guard it, and only sent him on other errands after you arrived at the boat; even if he boarded the wrong boat, nothing would have been lost. Now that this has happened, it is simply your fate to lose the money—how can you blame the servant?" They were both released without further depositions.

Note: When goods are loaded onto a boat, they must never be left unattended. One must guard against the helmsman stealing and also ensure a clever servant is present for good fortune. Thus, when an inexperienced servant carries the travel bundle—the very thing that holds the silver and goods—he must stay by your side, and you must entrust it only to a reliable place; then nothing will be lost. If you first order him to carry it ahead and it is mistakenly left on another boat, how can there be no loss? Yet Menglin knew only how to reminisce about old times, causing his servant to lose the money by mistake and dragging them into a lawsuit—how foolish! All merchants should take this as a warning.

stories.title_en: A Porter Runs Off with Goods Fresh off the Boat

paragraphs.en: By the creek at Jianning city, whenever a merchant boat reaches shore, porters swarm and beg to be hired to carry loads into the city. An experienced traveler will always shout the crowd of porters back, wait until the boat's goods are all brought ashore and counted and recorded, then divide them into several loads, call several porters he can recognize, send them into the city, and at once have someone follow behind; only then is there no loss. If a greenhorn arrives, the porters, without waiting to see whether the things have been fully checked, load them onto the carriers at once; and if you hurry after the porters, you often leave things still on the boat not yet brought in.

There was a licentiate named Tian from Houguan County who went out to tutor. At year's end he returned home with more than forty taels of teaching silver and another ten-odd taels worth of clothes and bedding, packed into two large baskets. Passing through Jiancheng, he wished to enter and visit a fellow townsman, so he ordered a porter to carry the baskets ahead. As a Confucian scholar, Tian followed slowly behind. The porter, seeing him lagging, walked faster and faster, hurried into the city gate; in the crowded throng, he moved even quicker, carrying the load into a winding alley and fled. Though Tian called from behind, "Stop!" how could he stop him? Inside the city, the winding alleys forked many ways—where could one search? The next day, he presented the matter to Prefectural Constable Lü.

Constable Lü was a sharp official. To catch a porter who had cheated out of goods, you must use porters to find him. He at once called two runners: "You mark this Licentiate Tian. This afternoon he will wear a white long gown on a boat. When luggage arrives, a porter will surely make off with it; you two follow secretly behind and seize him at his house." He then said to the licentiate: "Today get a dummy load of luggage, board a boat ten li out, and come to the prefecture. When you reach shore as you did the other day, call a porter to carry it. Wear a white long gown so these two runners can recognize you. If they are already beside you, walk slowly on purpose and let this porter carry it off; they will surely catch the earlier porter." The licentiate did not yet see his meaning.

That same afternoon, he packed his luggage, took a boat from ten li away, and arrived. Seeing the two runners beside him, each recognized the other, so he called a porter to carry the luggage and followed slowly behind. The porter indeed made off with it. The two runners trailed him to his house and caught him, saying: "Constable Lü wants you." The porter, Huang San, unaware of the situation, had no choice but to go along. Constable Lü asked: "Why did you run off with the licentiate's luggage?" Startled, Huang San replied: "I only left it at my house temporarily and intended to return it." The official shouted, "Beat him five strokes!" Licentiate Tian then arrived at the yamen. Constable Lü instructed Huang San: "Today I spare your punishment. Yesterday a porter stole one load of Master Tian's goods. You have two days to track him down; if you cannot find him, you will be held liable for the loss." Huang San said: "River porters change shifts every two days. Yesterday was not our shift." Constable Lü replied: "Then you must investigate yesterday's men."

Huang San conducted a secret investigation for two days but found nothing. On the third day, officials arrived to arrest him. Halfway there, he spotted a porter named Liu Wu exchanging three qian of silver for cash, then immediately buying fish, meat, and other items to take home. Huang San had Liu Wu seized and brought to the yamen, reporting: "I found nothing during my search. However, I just encountered Liu Wu changing money and purchasing a large quantity of fish and meat; this behavior seems suspicious." The constable promptly dispatched four men, who accompanied Licentiate Tian and Huang San directly to Liu Wu's house to search. They found only a small room, but upon searching, they indeed discovered the stolen goods. Liu Wu was taken to the constable's yamen, where he confessed: "The silver and goods are here. For the past five days, I dared not leave home. Today, I merely used three qian of silver to exchange for cash and buy provisions to celebrate. Yes, I committed the crime of abduction and theft." The constable ordered twenty strokes and declared: "Both of you porters stole a traveler's belongings; each should be sentenced to penal servitude. However, since Huang San caught Liu Wu, his involvement is redeemed. Give him ten additional strokes and release him as a warning for future cases. Considering Liu Wu is a poor man, I will sentence him only for committing an improper act. Once the fine is paid, he may go free." He then instructed Licentiate Tian to submit a receipt, after which all the original goods were returned to him. Within a few days, the true thief and the genuine loot were apprehended. Without exceptional administrative talent, how could such a result have been achieved?

Note: Porters running off with goods happen everywhere, so travelers must be most vigilant. As for Constable Lü, who uncovered the deceit and captured the thief without sparing any effort, the whole matter hinged on one move: using a porter to catch a porter. This is what is meant by "using barbarians to fight barbarians." The proverb also says, "A thief catches a thief; use a needle to pick out a splinter"—the same idea. Those who hire porters should take this as a warning; those who hunt thieves may take it as a model.
